Breaking.title: Planning permission granted for MoD Bicester asylum centre plans
Breaking.text:
Planning permission to house asylum seekers at a former military site near the Oxfordshire village of Piddington has been granted by the government.

The Home Office's application to house up to 1,256 men at the MoD Bicester site was fast-tracked using an Urgent Crown Development application.

The nearby village of Piddington symbolically voted to leave the UK in opposition to the planned site, which has also been legally challenged by campaigners.

A Home Office spokesperson said the planning permission "allows us to continue to progress the use of MoD Bicester" but no final decision on the proposal had been taken.

A government report said the decision received 3,177 representations against, and one in support.

It also said Housing Secretary Angela Rayner ruled permission should be granted because "national demand for asylum accommodation remains high".

The permission allows for demolition of existing buildings, the erection of new modular accommodation, and provisions for health and welfare facilities.

Shadow home secretary Chris Philp said: "Angela Rayner and the Labour government have betrayed the people of Piddington by abusing their emergency powers in this way."

He continued: "Instead of accommodating illegal immigrants, the government should leave the ECHR so they can be rapidly deported."

Liberal Democrat MP for Bicester and Woodstock Calum Miller said it was "the wrong plan and the wrong site for local communities, asylum seekers and taxpayers".

"I am deeply disappointed that the government has approved this proposal despite the serious concerns raised by residents and local councils as well as the major problems with the site," he added.

The approval could be challenged by an application to the High Court within six weeks, beginning the day after the date of the decision.

The government said a challenge "may be brought only on the ground that the decision is legally flawed; it is not an opportunity to reconsider the planning merits".

Breaking.title: Junior doctor burnout may put maternity patients at risk, regulator warns
Breaking.text:
Training doctors working on maternity wards are experiencing high rates of burnout which could have a "critical impact" on patients, a regulator is warning.

The General Medical Council (GMC) says the fully qualified doctors, who are still training in obstetrics and gynaecology, are reporting more feelings of overwork and sleep deprivation than similar trainees in any other field of medicine or surgery, and are also more wary of escalating concerns.

Author Adam Kay, who left medicine in 2010 after dealing with a traumatic birth incident, says the report "makes for miserable reading" and says "nothing has been done" to improve workplace culture.

The Department for Health and Social Care said ensuring every maternity unit "meets the highest standards" was a priority.

The GMC analysed figures from its national training survey, which in 2026 was completed by 68% of trainee doctors, which includes registrars, representing almost 52,000 people.

Almost one in three trainee doctors working in obstetrics and gynaecology felt hesitant or apprehensive approaching a senior colleague about a patient, compared with one in five across all specialties

They were also more likely to be at moderate to high risk of burnout - 70% versus 61% across all specialties

One in three said they regularly suffered from sleep deprivation compared to one in five across the wider pool of trainees

Charlie Massey, head of the GMC, said having doctors who feel they cannot speak up, could have a critical impact on patients.

"Creating environments where staff are supported, listened to and feel able to raise concerns is essential."

He told the BBC: "Sadly, when we see when things go wrong, it is it is very often because of failures in terms of culture and leadership."

Author Adam Kay says the findings echo his own time as a doctor.

He went on to write This is going to hurt: Secret Diaries of a junior doctor about his experiences, including caring for a mother who delivered a stillborn baby.

"I wasn't particularly well supported after it happened. It was a bit like I said I'd sprained my ankle or something. There was no talk of a debrief. There was no offer of time off or counselling. It's just, you know, get on with it."

He described the GMC report as "pretty miserable reading" and suggested that nothing had changed since he left the profession 16 years ago.

"The doctors working on our labour wards are burnt out, bullied, don't feel like they can report problems upstream. It's upsetting to read."

Aside from a negative work culture, a key problem, Kay suggests, is lack of staffing.

"There are fewer staff on the wards than ever. I can't remember the last time I spoke to a doctor in that specialty who wasn't working out what their plan B was, whether that's going part time, moving to another country, or moving to the pharmaceutical industry.

"It will always be busy and high pressured, but there are things you can affect. You can affect the number of people who are working there and you can affect the culture. You should be able to speak to your boss. You should be able to go and take a break and go for a cup of tea or a wee, and that's not the case at the moment."

Dr Miriam Broughton, 27, is a resident doctor in her second year of training to become an obstetrics and gynaecology consultant.

While the decisions she has to make sometimes keep her awake at night, she says she wouldn't change her job for the world.

"Being there to deliver someone's baby at the best moment of their life is honestly one of the best things you could ever do. And then also working with people through the hardest moments of their lives and being able to support them is just priceless."

The main challenge, she says, are the sheer number of demands placed on a doctor in her field.

"It could be that there's two or three ladies whose babies need delivering, and then somebody else coming in on maternity triage whose baby isn't moving, and you might also be getting calls from A&E about a lady having a miscarriage who's bleeding really heavily.

"There's just one of you to manage all those jobs."

Broughton says while she has largely had positive experiences, it is important to step back and look at the wider culture.

"You do hear things from other hospitals about people feeling nervous about calling the consultant...which isn't great."

Dr Kat Barton, chair of the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RCOG) National Trainee Committee, says workplace issues end up affecting patients.

"Many of us feel overstretched and close to burnout. This reflects staff shortages, working beyond our hours, and knowing that despite our best efforts, the care women receive is being affected.

"We know the safest care comes from teams that are well-supported, well-resourced, and listen to each other and to women and families.

"We need the government to invest in safe staffing at every level, protect our time for training, and support our wellbeing and careers, so we can give women the safe, compassionate care they deserve."

Recent high profile maternity reviews, which looked at outcomes for mothers and babies, also highlighted concerns about workplace culture, leadership and the ability of staff to raise concerns.

Obstetrics and gynaecology trainees were more positive than average about some aspects of patient safety reporting, the GMC survey indicated, including how to report patient safety incidents and near misses.

A DHSC spokesperson said: "In all the investigations carried out in recent years into failings in maternity services, one of the key lessons has been that members of staff must feel empowered to speak up if they have concerns about workload, or patient safety, and their concerns must be acted upon.

"All NHS trusts are now required to have a dedicated Freedom to Speak Up Guardian and internal pathways for staff to raise concerns about the working environment, patient safety, or their own wellbeing.

"Alongside this, we are continuing to grow and strengthen the workforce to help relieve the pressures on busy maternity units, and there are now a record number of midwives working in the NHS, with over 600 added in the past year.

"Since coming into the role in July, the Secretary of State has made maternity services a personal priority, and the Maternity and Neonatal Taskforce that she is chairing is working to respond to the concerns raised by staff and families alike, and ensure that every maternity unit meets the highest standards of patient safety and care."

Breaking.title: Zelensky welcomes US bringing Europe into Russia-Ukraine peace talks
Breaking.text:
Ukraine's president has welcomed a pledge from US envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, to include delegates from the European Union in the next round of peace talks with Russia.

European leaders have expressed deepening security concerns this week, and Volodymyr Zelensky said bringing them into the talks would ensure the EU has a "voice" in negotiations.

Kushner and Witkoff met Zelensky in Dublin on Thursday evening as part of a busy day of shuttle diplomacy - they met Vladimir Putin in Moscow earlier, who said that Russia's position on the war - and its demand for territory - has not changed.

The meetings follow talks in Abu Dhabi last week that failed to reach a breakthrough in ending the war.

But Thursday did see Russia and Ukraine agree to another prisoner exchange - the largest swap yet since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.

Kushner said it would return "thousands of people to their families", but further details like how many prisoners would be exchanged or a timeline, were not given.

Zelensky has for several years been calling for European delegates to be included in the peace talks, and says it makes sense because of Kyiv's longer-term ambition to join the European Union.

On Thursday, Kushner said that the US has been "working very, very closely over the past several months with Europeans and I think that that's been very important."

He added that he had stressed to Putin how important it is to have European delegates "at the table".

"He's willing to give it a try," Kushner added.

Ukraine and Europe have long been concerned about the current US government's commitment to European security and its softening towards the Kremlin.

Moscow has been dismissive of European involvement, although Europeans have long argued that they are central to any post-war dynamics on their continent.

Earlier on Thursday, Vice President of the European Commission Kaja Kallas, the EU's top diplomat, told BBC's Newshour the presence of a European delegate showed the Kremlin "now realised that Europe is a big player".

Kallas also expressed doubts that there was Russian momentum towards a peace deal.

Taoiseach (Irish Prime Minister) Micheál Martin told a host of Euro leaders gathered in the Irish capital on Thursday that he believed the security of the region has been "fundamentally reshaped" by Russia's war.

"Many member states [of the EU] feel an existential threat because of what has happened in Ukraine and the potential, if Ukraine was to fall, for further aggression on the European continent," he told reporters.

Approximately one-fifth of Ukraine remains under control of Russian forces, and cross-border incursions are increasingly common.

Tensions between the US and Ukraine were on display on Thursday before Witkoff and Kushner's meeting with Zelensky.

Earlier, the Ukrainian leader said that the military was facing more "systematic" restrictions to Starlink's military-grade satellite service, Starshield, meaning Kyiv was struggling to intercept Russian jet-powered drones.

The technology owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX company has played a vital role in government and military connectivity in Ukraine, and increasingly assists in facilitating communication on Ukraine's front line.

Breaking.title: The school where white working-class pupils defy the odds
Breaking.text:
Two years ago, I stood in a school hall in Sunderland on GCSE results day and watched the pride and surprise in the faces of teenagers as the envelopes were opened.

Even after years of covering results days, I was emotional to see a set of outstanding results in a school facing so many challenges. Almost half of the school's pupils receive free school meals, meaning their parents are on low incomes. In fact, the results in the ex-mining town of Hetton-le-Hole were as strong as the most affluent parts of southern England.

This summer, Hetton Academy hit another milestone, with 80% of its pupils getting a pass of at least a grade 4 in maths and English. A grade 4 is roughly equivalent to a 'C' under the old system, and is seen as a passport to jobs and further education.

Another striking detail about Hetton is that almost all of its pupils are from a white, working-class background, a group that's been in the spotlight for some time. This week saw the launch of the second phase of an independent inquiry, led by former Cabinet minister Baroness Morris, into why children from those communities lag behind their peers at school. Education Secretary Lucy Powell said: "Right now, too many white, working-class children are falling behind at every stage of their education."

But Hetton Academy seems to have defied the odds. The school's principal, Vicky Pinkney, refuses to accept low incomes should mean low results. "I don't think we should be accepting less just because of the community you work in," she says.

The stellar results have won Hetton a place among an elite group of schools: mainstream secondaries that don't select pupils academically, and where 80% of pupils get that all-important grade 4 in maths and English.

In fact, there were only 339 non-selective schools in England that hit an average 80% pass rate in maths and English for the three years to 2025, out of around 3,000 that published the relevant data. High achieving schools have been the focus of some political attention recently, with MPs in several parties arguing that we should study them closely.

What can they tell us about how to raise standards? And could other schools facing the same challenges as Hetton achieve equally impressive results?

From a quick glance of those 339 high-achieving schools, it becomes clear that some of their success comes from things that are difficult to shift.

In particular, the economic profile of the pupils clearly matters. Schools that hit the average 80% pass rate have fewer children from the lowest-income families than average, and are less likely to be in deprived areas. They also have fewer children with special educational needs.

Analysts say we shouldn't be surprised by the huge role played by family finances in determining a school's outcome.

Prof John Jerrim, an academic at University College London who researches education systems in different countries, says that England's system is failing poorer pupils.

Since 2010, even while an overhaul of GCSEs has been widely seen as raising standards, the likelihood of the children from the poorest families passing these key exams has barely changed, he says.

"It's really hard to move the dial," says Prof Jerrim.

Seamus Murphy, CEO of Turner Schools, which runs schools in financially deprived areas, thinks the push for higher academic standards under Michael Gove from 2010 instilled "vision and challenge" into the system. But it doesn't work for all pupils, he says.

Especially in places where families are struggling with the cost of living, he says, an 18-year-old earning the minimum wage was "a big deal", and it might be tempting for some parents to push their children towards work rather than education.

The high-performing schools on our list also have a lower proportion of pupils from a White British background than other schools. Earlier this year, Baroness Morris's inquiry, external found that many white, working-class families have simply lost faith in the school system and increasingly believe it does not guarantee future success.

So it's clear that a school's fortunes are shaped in part by factors outside its control.

But there's a complication. When you zoom in on particular schools, some of them do seem to be able to defy gravity, achieving high results despite seemingly being on the 'wrong' side of those demographic factors.

So back to that school in Sunderland. It stands out as something of an exception: it has a mostly white, working-class population, and lots of pupils from poor families. In fact, if you just look at the very highest grades, the region in which Hetton sits came bottom of the English league table this year. Just 3% of GCSEs in the North East were given the top mark (a grade 9) this summer, versus 8% in London, according to exam watchdog Ofqual. (On other measures of GCSE performance, the North East ranked more favourably.)

So, what is the school doing right?

After opening in the 1960s under the name Hetton School, it struggled for years with low performance. Hetton-le-Hole town was hit hard by the closure of the Eppleton mine in the 1980s. It became common for families to send their children elsewhere in search of a good education. An Ofsted report in 2021 ranked the school as "requires improvement". That was the last report before it converted into an academy.

But by 2024, Ofsted said it was "rapidly improving". This year's 80% pass rate for maths and English GCSEs ranks the school high within the Sunderland local authority, and well above the average for England, where 57% passed maths and 60% passed English.

It's now the "school of choice" for local families, says the principal, Pinkney.

The school also says it aims to have a warm, welcoming ethos.

For Year 11 pupils, there is a separate entrance path which is lined each morning by teachers who stop a few and quiz them about their subject, problem solving on the spot with a whiteboard.

While it's done in a good-humoured way, the decision on who to stop for this brief intervention is discussed at regular review meetings.

There is more structured support for everyone in the form of an hour of extra study four days a week after school. If maths is where you are stuck, you might do two of these hours on that subject.

Over the run-up to exams, the school holds 'Revision Sundays', when the Year 11 pupils can come in for a top-up session and eat a roast lunch together.

It's all designed to foster a feeling of inclusion in the classroom, which in turn can boost exam grades, the school thinks. And it seems to be working. When reviewing the school in 2024, Ofsted praised the "positive relationships" enjoyed between pupils and staff.

And a government-commissioned study, published this year by the University of Cambridge, found that pupils who say they "belong" in school see "significantly higher attainment" in their GCSEs.

Around this time of year at Hetton, parents of Year 11 pupils, who will sit exams next summer, receive an invitation to a 'Fish and Tips' evening at the school. They'll get advice on what they can do as parents to support learning and a bag full of revision resources. Booklets and stationery are tailored to each pupil.

Afterwards Pinkney and the other staff sit down with them for fish and chips in the canteen, paid for by the school. The parents see her as "just another Mam", she says, who wants their children to do their best. She says some of the parents may have had a poor experience of school, or simply been able to get into work without many qualifications themselves.

It's a community that mostly "stays in the area", Pinkney says, and it's the school's task to "open their horizons".

But still, challenges remain. It certainly won't be easy for every school in a white, working-class area to emulate Hetton's success.

Prof Lindsey Macmillan, an expert in how education shapes life chances, was involved in the recent inquiry into white working-class children.

The pupils start school already behind, she says, and that gap only widens through secondary school due to a growing disengagement with education.

The inquiry found "telling" evidence that the connection with school "falls off a cliff" for white working-class families at the point of moving to secondary school, leading to poor attendance.

Parents told the inquiry things like, "I didn't need qualifications" to get into work - the same message as Pinkney hears from some parents in Hetton-le-Hole. (In reality, Macmillan says, formal qualifications are now more important for getting a job than they were in previous decades, when there were more routes into well-paid industrial work, and more on-the-job training.)

That's a point supported by Prof Jerrim, who thinks schools should get families to buy-in on education by clearly explaining to them how qualifications can help their children find work.

The inquiry also reported a sense of white working-class parents not wanting their children to leave their area, with its strong sense of connection. England's education system was described as being out-of-step with the values of white, working-class communities. Parents in those areas are ambitious for their children, the inquiry found, but often prioritise happiness and life-readiness alongside or above high grades.

Breaking.title: Andy Burnham says 'win-win' deal can be agreed between UK and EU
Breaking.text:
Andy Burnham said he believes a "win-win" deal can be agreed with the European Union, adding it could be "more like the Brexit that people thought they were voting for" in 2016.

The prime minister is exploring closer ties with the bloc and is expected to sign new agreements on food, energy and youth mobility at a UK-EU summit on 20 November.

Speaking after meeting European leaders in Ireland on Thursday, Burnham said he hopes a deal could help lower prices and boost the UK economy. He predicted the negotiations could "go down to the wire".

The Conservatives have previously said Labour are "dragging us into the European Union via the back door with their EU reset".

While Burnham has argued that Brexit has done "more harm than good", he has ruled out major changes to the UK's relationship with the EU before the next general election.

Labour's 2024 general election manifesto pledged there would be "no return to the single market, the customs union, or freedom of movement", and Burnham has committed to this.

The manifesto also said the party wanted to "make Brexit work" and reset the UK's relationship with the EU.

Former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer struck a deal in May 2025 covering fishing, trade and other areas and next week's summit will see the UK government seek to agree further changes.

Burnham has also made clear he wants to examine the "pros and cons" of the options for Britain's long-term relationship with the bloc.

Speaking to reporters on Thursday, Burnham was asked to explain if his decision to reopen the debate on the UK's future with Europe had helped or hindered the negotiations linked to the summit.

Burnham replied "I think it has helped" before adding: "We've got a big week ahead of us to try and get this deal over the line.

"But let's be clear what's at stake: what we can achieve through this deal is lower prices for British consumers, lower costs for British businesses, more growth in our economy so there's really big prizes here, and I will fight now over the days to come to make sure we get this deal over the line."

Pressed on whether discounted university tuition fees for European students would be part of the deal, Burnham said "requests are coming from the European side, we are putting our requests on the table too".

He added: "I believe there is a good deal to be done that could be a win-win for Britain and Europe. I think it actually could be more like the Brexit that people thought they were voting for in 2016."

Ahead of the summit, the UK and EU agreed a draft deal on removing post-Brexit checks from food and agriculture exports.

Similar texts for deals on emissions trading and a youth travel and work scheme have also been circulated to EU nations.

As a result of the agreement, the government claims the UK economy will eventually see £5.1bn worth of annual benefits.

Burnham also told MPs last month that the summit presents an opportunity to make progress on "controlling illegal immigration".

Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch has previously strongly opposed any move to align with EU rules, saying it would "actually take us backwards".

On Thursday, Conservative MP and former minister Dame Priti Patel said: "Andy Burnham's obsession with the EU risks dragging Britain backwards, damaging our economy and leaving hardworking British taxpayers footing the bill."

The Liberal Democrats earlier this month described the draft deal as a "patch, not a fix" and said the "real solution is to re-join the single market and to establish a customs union with the EU".

Reform UK believes one of the "key benefits" of Brexit is that Britain no longer has to "adhere to ridiculous EU rules" and any form of alignment could have a negative impact on the country's trade policy.

The Green Party has called for the UK to re-join the customs union, with leader Zack Polanski previously saying "full membership of the EU remains the best option for the UK".

Breaking.title: Russian warship hit by Ukrainian drone in Gulf of Finland
Breaking.text:
Finnish officials have confirmed that a Russian warship was attacked in the Gulf of Finland on Wednesday, although little is known about the strike.

Ukraine's SBU security service said it targeted the ship Naro-Fominsk as part of a broader drone operation against Russia's Ust-Luga oil export depot on the Baltic coast.

The attack, thought to be the first time Ukrainian drones have attacked a Russian ship in an area of the Baltic Sea open to civilian maritime traffic, has raised questions about whether Ukraine could expand its strikes.

Helsinki has been one of Kyiv's closest European allies, and Finnish officials have described the incident as a direct result of Russia's continued full-scale war.

Finland's military has given few details of the incident, but it appears to have taken place in a narrow stretch some distance from the Finnish coast.

The country's Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen was adamant that the situation in the Baltic Sea remained stable and safe and that there was no threat of any kind to marine traffic.

Defence officials are understood to have stressed to Kyiv that the Gulf is a relatively narrow waterway used by oil tankers and civilian vessels, and is also home to subsea data cables.

Ukraine's SBU described the Russian ship as a Buyan-M type small corvette that carried Kalibr and Oniks cruise missiles. There were also unconfirmed reports of Russian combat helicopters being destroyed.

Martin Herem, the defence minister of Estonia, which borders the Gulf, told public broadcaster ERR that the ship was hit at about 05:30 (03:30 GMT) on Wednesday but did not say how it was attacked: "We know that smoke came from the ship afterwards. The ship itself went back towards St Petersburg."

The extent of casualties or damage sustained by the Russian navy ship remains unclear, and Moscow rarely gives such details.

Breaking.title: Pat Cummins calls Usman Khawaja sandpaper claims 'wrong' and 'nonsense'
Breaking.text:
Australia captain Pat Cummins has hit back at former team-mate Usman Khawaja's claims over the sandpaper scandal, calling them "100% wrong" and "utter nonsense".

In 2018, Steve Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft were punished for a plot to tamper with the ball using sandpaper in Australia's Test against South Africa in Cape Town.

Khawaja has published his autobiography this week and the former batter has said the entire Australia team, which included Cummins, knew about the sandpaper scheme and should have taken responsibility.

But in an extraordinary 68-minute address to the media in Sydney, Cummins countered and said: "When he says we all knew, if by that he means we knew sandpaper was going out on the field, he's 100% wrong.

"I said that consistently for the last eight years. I did not know that was happening.

"He says that I and others were architects of a scheme to ball tamper with sandpaper. That's complete and utter nonsense."

Cummins and Khawaja played 56 Tests together until Khawaja retired from international cricket in January.

Khawaja was in the Australia XI when Cummins made his Test debut in 2011 and the pair were also once team-mates in domestic cricket with New South Wales.

"Usman is a friend, but friends aren't casual with each other's lives and reputations," said Cummins.

"In his book he's been casual with my life and the lives of many others - and, I think, Australian cricket.

"I support him to tell his story, 100%, I'm glad he feels like he can, but we have to be accountable for the things that we say and do."

In a media conference he arranged himself, Cummins began by promising to answer all questions because, he said: "I don't want to talk about this again after today."

At times emotional, Cummins addressed a wide range of topics, including:

Advice that some of Khawaja's claims are defamatory, but he will not take legal action

He had been in contact with Khawaja and Smith since the book was published, but not Warner

His belief that the one-year bans handed to Smith and Warner, and a nine-month suspension to Bancroft were "heavy handed"

He had no recollection of Australia tampering with the ball in the 2017-18 Ashes series against England

He had met with Cricket Australia chief executive Todd Greenberg, who has reviewed the files from the original investigation

Explaining why sandpaper would have been present in the dressing room and that it was sometimes used by bowlers in training in order to practise with a reverse-swinging ball

Khawaja's allegations have reopened the debate about the sandpaper plot, the investigation into the cheating, the culture of Australian cricket and the reputations of those involved.

The story has dominated the media in Australia and caused headlines around the cricketing world.

Khawaja has been supported by Warner and Chadd Sayers, a seam bowler who was part of the Australia squad on the 2018 tour of South Africa.

However, his allegations have been rejected by Darren Lehmann, who was then the Australia head coach and former England batter Graeme Hick, one of Lehmann's assistants. Mitchell Starc, another bowler on the tour, has also denied Khawaja's claims.

Khawaja has put a spotlight on Cummins and his fellow bowlers Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon. The four were Australia's attack in Cape Town and remain their first-choice bowlers eight years later.

The quartet have always denied any knowledge of the plot, including in the release of a joint-statement in 2021.

In his book - Sabr - Khawaja alleged Australia were urged to find ways of getting the ball to swing by a coach, while Bancroft was later encouraged to cheat.

Khawaja also said he asked for the entire team to take responsibility for the controversy in Cape Town, but his request was rejected by two unnamed players.

Cummins said he does not recall any suggestion that the team should have shared the responsibility, or that it was rejected.

On the idea that the whole team were aligned in a plot to tamper with the ball, he said: "There was no masterplan around using illegal methods. People assume you've gone from very legal methods to suddenly taking sandpaper, and there must have been some huge masterplan.

"That is not the case. There's no grand plan. There's no team meeting. There's no bowlers saying this is what must happen."

"There's big leaps where Usman is being vague."

In his book, Khawaja detailed how he was not interviewed as part of the investigation despite sitting next to Bancroft in the changing rooms during the Test at Newlands.

Both Khawaja and Warner have criticised the investigation, which Greenberg has said he will not reopen.

Cummins confirmed he has met with Greenberg and, although the captain said he did not want to break a "confidence", that Greenberg has reviewed the sandpaper files since the release of Khawaja's book and found the accounts in the investigation to be "consistent".

Cummins has played 77 Tests for Australia and has been captain sine 2021. He said he has seen only one instance of ball-tampering in his career, during a domestic Sheffield Shield match, when a player took a bottletop on to the field.

However, he did admit that balls can sometimes be altered during training sessions, if bowlers want to practise in a certain way, or batters want to face a ball of a particular condition.

Cummins said it was not unknown for training balls to be scuffed in such circumstances, using sandpaper or even a Stanley knife.

When it was put to Cummins that he, as a bowler, must have suspected that the Cape Town ball had been tampered with, the 33-year-old described that bowlers often touch a ball as little as possible, in order to keep it dry and in a state where it will reverse-swing.

At the time of the sandpaper scandal, Cummins was 24 and playing in his 13th Test. Asked about a potential culture of ball-tampering in that era, Cummins said he noticed things then that he now realises could have been cheating.

On why Khawaja has chosen to speak now, at the end of his career, rather than in the intervening eight years, Cummins said the episode could have "weighed heavy" on the left-hander.

Addressing the culture of the Australia team eight years ago, Cummins said: "I didn't like the way we spoke to umpires, the opposition. I think there was a bit of an arrogance and a bit of an ugliness at times that didn't sit well with me as a young guy.

"Now I'm captain, I have spent a lot of time making sure that that's not the case."

Speaking about Cummins' news conference on Fox Cricket, where he is working as an analyst for Australia's one-day series against England which got under way on Friday, Warner said: "I stick with Uzzie. It's the truth. The captain threw Uzzie under the bus.

"We've got to live with the consequence daily. I feel it was a botched investigation. To get it over and done with. This won't rest.

"I'm not going to accept [things] until the truth is out."

Facing more than a dozen TV cameras, and a gaggle of reporters several times as large, Cummins answered questions for over an hour - determined to put so-called "sandpapergate" to rest.

He was patient and cautious, pausing often to consider his responses and to make sure they answered the questions being asked of him, even at one point shooing away a minder from Cricket Australia who tried to wrap things up.

Cummins was careful in his criticism of Khawaja, despite needling questions from the media gathered, but he was also frank - using strong words to reject his claims and admitting he was annoyed Khawaja had put him in this position.

He spoke of a mix of amusement and uneasiness at the camera crews now parked outside his house.

He rejected media speculation that his captaincy could be under threat. He admitted he was struggling to reconcile his years-long friendship with Khawaja with the events of the past week: "That's something I've been grappling with the last couple of days... friends aren't casual with each other's lives and reputations."

But gesturing to the Sheffield Shield match going on outside the batting nets, and referencing the ODI about to begin in Perth, he said he was also incredibly frustrated that the sandpapergate scandal is still a distraction for Australian cricket.

"It's been eight years. We're moving on. So ‌you have got to draw a line at some point."

Breaking.title: Russell Brand will face 'hell on earth' in Wandsworth prison, says ex inmate
Breaking.text:
Russell Brand will face "hell on earth" inside HMP Wandsworth, a former inmate at the London prison has said.

Brand, 51, was convicted a week ago of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault and was sentenced on Monday to 10 years and six months in prison.

He is currently being held at the South London jail, which is one of England's largest Victorian-era prisons.

Chris Atkins, who served eight months at HMP Wandsworth for tax fraud, described the prison as "hell on earth".

He continued: "The first month is hands-down the worst. The mental shock is absolutely colossal. It was colossal for me and it's going to be 10 times worse for him because of the nature of his offences and the height from which he's fallen.

"He has to come to terms with it and the pure physical shock of suddenly being trapped in a dungeon for weeks on end with nobody to talk to most of the time is ghastly."

A source close to the disgraced comedian said he was doing "remarkably well considering the circumstances" and that he had been moved from isolation to a main wing in the prison.

A member of staff at Wandsworth said there was "much excitement" among the inmates about Brand's arrival.

"Prisons are boring and Russell Brand being in their space has given them some fun - they've been slamming on cell doors and shouting out his name. He is a rapist, so there's also been some anger about what he's done.

"We're very aware of that feeling," they said.

Brand is likely to still be in a cell on his own. It would usually have a bed, a basin and a toilet. He may have a television and kettle depending on where in the prison he is housed.

On arrival, Brand's possessions will have been confiscated. That will include his mobile phone, clothing, and any other valuables. He will have been issued with a grey prison tracksuit - a uniform that has been described by some of those who've been inside as "itchy" and "often the wrong size".

The former media personality and comedian will have been given a night pack. It contains items such as biscuits, teabags, a small bag of cereal, some sugar and a carton of milk. According to the charity, Prison Reform Trust, this is to help inmates until they can buy goods from the prison shop.

Brand, who has positioned himself as a Christian influencer, would be able to register for the weekly Sunday service in the prison chapel, inmates said.

"Many sign up just to get out of their cell," one added. They said Brand could probably get regular time with the prison chaplain, if he wanted.

Inmates receive money through prison work or from their family. But several former prisoners have told the BBC there are a limited number of jobs in places like workshops, laundry rooms and libraries.

They say it is much harder for sex offenders to get work because their conviction means they are more at risk of assault from mixing with other inmates.

Staff at other prisons say Brand's fame and the offences he has been convicted of could make him a target among other inmates.

Sex offenders are often among those most at risk of being attacked. One prison governor said: "When a trial gets plenty of publicity it highlights the crimes the offender has committed.

"This in turn makes him vulnerable to the inmates own 'justice' system of arbitrary beatings and assaults, especially where sex crimes are involved."

The prison paperwork is also said to be a huge challenge for newcomers. Getting permission to make phone calls and filling out visitor requests can take a long time and have to go through the system to be signed off.

Atkins said: "He won't have anyone set up on his visitor account - visitors need a series of checks. Phone numbers need to be approved. These checks are not quick and you need to know how to make these applications.

"There is often nobody there to tell you how this all works so you have to work it out." He said it took five weeks to see his young son.

It's just days since Brand was sentenced to more than a decade in prison.

At this stage nobody knows what the future holds for him. In time he may be transferred to a different jail with a less harsh regime and more modern facilities.

The guidelines state offenders jailed for four years or more for some serious violent or sexual offences will be released at the two-thirds point. In Brand's case that would be seven years.

Breaking.title: Poundland gets more time to secure a rescue deal as emergency talks continue
Breaking.text:
Poundland has avoided immediate collapse after a deadline was extended to find a rescue deal.

A deadline to secure a buyer for the retail chain was set to expire at midnight, but a court has given Poundland an extra 10 days to find a buyer.

The discount chain, which has 11,000 employees, has been edging towards administration after being blocked by owners Gordon Brothers from accessing cash in its bank accounts.

A committee of MPs questioned Gordon Brothers following accusations that the investment firm hoped to profit from selling off Poundland's 600 shops and stock piecemeal.

Gordon Brothers - which bought the chain for just £1 last year - is accused of forcing that outcome by restricting Poundland's access to available cash needed to restock shops, and pay wages and rent, ahead of the crucial Christmas trading period.

The investment firm, which specialises in buying and restructuring distressed companies, has denied the claims.

However, pressure remains on Poundland's owners after a takeover bid was rejected. The decision prompted calls for answers from politicians, including Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

About £50m had been frozen by Gordon Brothers, the BBC understands, meaning Poundland bosses were unable to restock shelves across its 600 shops.

The BBC understands that Gordon Brothers agreed to release a further £11m today from Poundland's accounts, on top of £10m announced earlier, as the firm seeks to find a new buyer.

Gordon Brothers said it was in talks with three parties for a sale of the whole business, and it had received "several offers from established high street retailers for significant parts of the business".

Following the meeting between MPs on the business and trade committee and representatives of Gordon Brothers, chairman Liam Byrne told the BBC that he was "deeply concerned" and described the firm's behaviour as "much like a wolf on Wall Street, on the British High Street".

"They refused to prioritise protecting jobs and stores over and above their own financial returns," he said.

"It's clear that they've taken millions out of Poundland at a time when they themselves said the business was on a knife edge."

Byrne said the committee's message to Gordon Brothers was to ensure Poundland had "access to the funds that it needs to trade at what should be one of the busiest periods in the year".

He urged Gordon Brothers to "do what is right to save jobs and stores and do that now".

"It's a good business, it's a much-loved business and, particularly in the middle of the cost of living crisis, communities up and down the country rely on access to the kind of stores that it operates," Byrne added.

Breaking.title: Suspected bomb hoax threats force fresh evacuations of Italian schools
Breaking.text:
Schools across Italy have received bomb threats for the second day in a row, sparking fresh panic and evacuations.

Some 3,778 schools, from Milan in the north to Sicily in the south, reported similar threats to one that created chaos on Wednesday - even though no explosive devices have been found.

The government has advised schools that "in the absence of concrete evidence beyond the simple receipt of a mass email indicating a danger, buildings must not not be evacuated". Unlike a day earlier, only 77 schools were evacuated on Thursday, authorities say.

Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni says her government will come up with "sector-specific" advice to help those facing this kind of threat.

Schools in Scotland and Northern Ireland received threats on Wednesday, too. It is unclear whether the incidents are connected.

On Thursday morning, a bomb alert at a Calais rail station delayed international and national train services in northern France.

The latest incidents follow a series of bomb hoaxes last week against airports and airlines in a number of European countries.

Although a number of threats were claimed by an extremist misogynistic group, it later denied any link to the false warnings.

Wednesday's email threat - sent to 6,300 out of a total of 7,476 Italian state schools - was said to be from a certain "Mikhail Andropov, leader of Vilayat di Misoginistan".

Some officials say it originated in Taiwan.

A similar message sent to Italian schools on Thursday, again signed by Mikhail Andropov, is said to have been sent from the account of a teacher in the Philippines whose account is believed to have been hacked.

Breaking.title: Sydney Swans players will not be charged after hotel incident, police say
Breaking.text:
Four top Australian Football League (AFL) players who were investigated in relation to an alleged sexual assault at a hotel in Melbourne earlier this year will not be charged, police have said.

After a "thorough investigation and based on legal advice" police would not proceed with criminal charges due to "insufficient evidence", police said in a statement.

Four Sydney Swans players - Isaac Heeney, James Jordon, Chad Warner and Nick Blakey, who now plays for North Melbourne - had been suspended for the rest of the season over the incident in August.

The men previously denied wrongdoing but apologised for breaching club standards by inviting women back to the hotel after a game and drinking.

Australian media reported that three women, understood to be adult entertainers, had alleged inappropriate touching during the incident at the Pullman Hotel and are looking into civil action.

"Due to the ongoing civil matter, Victoria Police is unable to make further comment," police said in a statement on Friday.

A fifth player, Riley Bice, who was also suspended by the club, had already been cleared by police.

A lawyer for one of the women said she was "devastated" by the police decision.

Jackson Pannam, of Slater and Gordon law firm, added that the move "does not amount to a finding that the incident our client reported did not occur, nor does it diminish the seriousness of what she says happened or its profound impact on her".

John Karantzis from Carbone Lawyers, acting for the other two women, told the ABC his clients were "very disappointed and distressed".

They would "vigorously pursue" a civil action, he said.

"My clients' civil claim is based on a different burden of proof, it is based on the balance of probabilities," he said.

Heeney welcomed the police announcement, saying the past three months had been "incredibly difficult for my family, [my fiancee] Steffie and those close to me".

"To my family and friends, your love and loyalty has meant more than words can do justice," he continued.

The Swans said in a statement that it had been "clear from the outset" that its decision to suspend the players was "separate from the police investigation, and it stands by that decision".

"The Club has commenced a comprehensive examination of its AFL program and is committed to acting on the findings and implementing meaningful change to build an environment that players, staff, members, supporters and corporate partners can be proud of," it said.

Swans CEO Matthew Pavlich told reporters it was "not a day for anyone to really celebrate" and "we're still looking very hard at the programme and understanding where we need to get better".

He said the club would be doing everything to "restore the standards that this club has held for a long period of time".

In a separate statement the AFL acknowledged the police decision and said it reserved the right to investigate should any further relevant information come to light.

Breaking.title: Hegseth awards medal to war memorial guard who reprimanded him and group
Breaking.text:
US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has awarded a medal to the guard who reprimanded his group at Arlington National Cemetery.

A video of a Veterans Day observance event on Wednesday showed Hegseth, his wife and senior advisers laughing and talking while posing for photos in front of the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier before the guard told them to be quiet.

In a statement, the Pentagon later announced that Hegseth had given Specialist Thomas Iglesias a Joint Service Commendation Medal "for the execution of his duties at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier".

Photos shared on the defence secretary's X account showed him presenting the medal to Iglesias.

He was accompanied by others whom the Pentagon identified as members of the 3rd US Infantry Regiment, known as the Old Guard, which is responsible for holding vigil over the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier.

"We love soldiers. We love standards. Well done, Specialist. Carry on Patriots," the accompanying text on Hegseth's post reads.

In the video, the army sentinel on duty later identified as Iglesias can be seen stepping towards Hegseth's group and shouting: "All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times."

The Arlington National Cemetery etiquette requests that visitors speak quietly and do not engage in disrespectful or disorderly conduct.

The tomb, which is one of the country's most sacred war memorials, marks the final resting place of an unknown soldier who was killed in World War One.

Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said in a statement: "While commemorating this solemn day, a soldier correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum.

"The Secretary and the entire Department have always honoured - and will always honour - the sacrifices our military men and women have made to keep America safe."

A service member from the 3rd Infantry Regiment stands watch over the tomb 24 hours a day and has done so since 1948.

It is not unusual for them to admonish visitors to the site, according to the BBC's US partner CBS News. They reportedly do so a few times a day.

Business.title: Why the UK economy is surprisingly resilient
Business.text:
The UK economy grew at its fastest rate for more than two years in the three months to September.

"Top gear" and "strikingly strong" were among the descriptions of the 0.7% growth offered by the economists who track every minor murmur of Britain's economy.

It is an upgrade on "solid" and "resilient", and in turn a world away from "hardest hit by the Iran War".

Against the backdrop of the world's biggest disruption to energy flows, rising market borrowing costs - and the cruel summers since the pandemic - it is impressive growth.

It should reset some of the swirl of self-reinforcing negativity.

The UK's economic growth has averaged less than 0.1% in the four Q3s [ie July to September] since the pandemic.

The average prediction just months ago for this July to September was just 0.1%.

Even the UK's official forecaster the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) effectively pencilled in 0.3% at the Budget just 3 weeks ago.

This figure has not been exceeded outside the pandemic since 2017. It puts the UK on course to be the second fastest growing economy after the US across the major G7 countries which also includes Canada, Japan, Germany, Italy and France.

It is tempting to think about what the economy would have done if the Iran War hadn't happened. If interest rates had been cut instead of their recent rise.

While the latest figure kills the doom, it is clearly not a boom either.

Spending on AI and tech have driven the surprise upside over the year. While the AI data centre boom may at any point turn to bust, these figures suggest that spending across the economy on investing in these technologies is helping to boost growth. Consumers have been resilient, at least till the autumn, perhaps helped by better economic vibes.

While there has been an understandable focus on high UK borrowing costs, another measure of the international standing of the UK economy, sterling's value, reached post Brexit referendum highs last week.

Productivity and investment is also looking stronger, especially after recent revisions. Some of the most encouraging figures are in private sector business investment.

I spoke to the chancellor at Nexeon in Oxfordshire, which is searching for a UK factory to manufacture its cutting edge electric vehicle battery - and British - technology. My colleagues visited British watchmakers in Maidenhead carving out a niche to take on the Swiss.

However, this may well not last for the final three months of the year.

Consumer confidence has already fallen as petrol and domestic energy prices start to rise again.

There is a significant challenge with everyday cost-of-living pressures in the coming months. Construction and private house building remain depressed.

The Iran conflict remains the big unknown and whether post the US midterm elections there could be a durable end to the conflict in the Gulf.

Some oil and gas production there is starting to normalise. It could bring down petrol prices, energy bills, government borrowing costs, and mortgage costs too.

Expect to see Downing Street investing heavily in "settlement of the conflict", which the chancellor told me is the "best economic policy".

Business.title: UK economy grows at fastest rate for more than two years
Business.text:
The UK economy grew at its fastest rate for more than two years in the three months to September.

Between July and September, the economy expanded by 0.7%, accelerating from the previous three months, official figures, external show.

The robust growth suggests a far more resilient economy than expected over the summer, despite the impact of higher energy prices from the Iran war.

Strong growth in the services sector - the largest part of the economy, which includes non-physical goods such as consultancy services and computer programming as well as hotels and restaurants - helped boost the numbers.

Within services, computer programming registered its fastest growth for the past three years, helped by cloud computing and AI-linked spending.

The boost from computer programming and consultancy services has been the biggest driver of growth so far this year.

Grant Fitzner, chief economist at the Office for National Statistics, said it was "possible growth could have been even stronger" if there hadn't been a war in the Middle East.

But he says households may still not feel better off, and that prices might soon start to rise more quickly than wages.

However, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the figures were "welcome news".

"Despite a year where events around the world have pushed up costs here at home, our economy is growing, bringing hope for the future," he said.

Chancellor John Healey told the BBC the figures showed a "remarkable resilience" in the face of global conflicts, and hopes they "bring back confidence in Britain".

Asked about how government decisions could be the reason for growth when AI investment has been a main driver, Healey said ministers can always "help or hinder" business confidence and investments.

Business.title: Some under-25s should get fewer benefits, Milburn review to say
Business.text:
Some young people could see reductions to the benefits they are entitled to under a radical overhaul of the welfare system to be recommended by a government-commissioned review.

As reported in the Times,, external Alan Milburn's year-long report, to be published on Tuesday, is expected to recommend moving under-25s off the main sickness and disability benefits.

Milburn, a former Labour health secretary, has been tasked by the government with helping reduce the one in eight 16 to 24 year-olds in the UK who are not in education, employment or training - otherwise known as "Neet".

He said on Wednesday night that his plans would not be "pain-free" and would affect both existing and new claimants.

His report is expected to say that under-25s should no longer be able to claim the health element of UK-wide universal credit - or personal independence payment (Pip), the main disability benefit in England and Wales.

Disabled people in Scotland can claim the devolved Adult Disability Payment.

Instead, under Milburn's plan, under-25s would receive an allowance on the same basic rate as universal credit.

Some could be eligible for a new "additional cost allowance" to cover day-to-day costs related to their conditions.

Some claimants would receive less under the plans - although the exact amounts will not be clear until early next year, when the government publishes legislation to implement the changes.

People can claim Pip to help them with the additional cost of being disabled or living with long-term physical or mental health conditions. It is available to those both in and out of work.

In his interim report,, external Milburn said survey data found that 19% of young people claiming disability or health benefits were in work.

Milburn, a Labour MP from 1992 to 2010, is also expected to recommend an investment of billions into more employment support for young people, including work placements, job subsidies and one-to-one personal advisers.

Those with more severe disabilities and unable to work would get a new benefit paid at a higher rate.

Milburn told the Times: "Candidly, it could mean that some people will get less financial support at the beginning of their benefit claim than under the current system.

"But actually, for young people, there's a different debate that we've got to resolve, which is whether the priority is their longer-term life chances or just their immediate shorter-term finances.

"I think what the current system does [is] it prioritises the latter over the former. I believe that's the wrong choice and it needs to be the other way around."

Speaking later on Thursday, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said young people would be given support "when they need it as teenagers rather than leaving them on benefits in their 20s".

He added: "The principle that we will be working on is that we will guarantee support for young people and that is the whole basis on which we will proceed."

Just under one million young people in the UK are Neets, data from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) from April to June suggests. This was a rise of 3% on the same period last year.

Milburn's recommendations are likely to be backed by Prime Minister Andy Burnham but could prove controversial among Labour MPs, who opposed welfare changes last year under his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer.

Dame Meg Hillier, who helped spearhead a backbench rebellion against Starmer's reforms, suggested she and her colleagues were broadly supportive this time around.

"What happened last year was a cut was being proposed and none of us could explain to people what would happen to them," the Labour MP told the BBC.

"Milburn has done some very good work on this so I'm giving him a fair wind," she added.

But Bell Ribeiro-Addy, one of the Labour backbenchers who revolted last year, said she was "not sure" she could vote to cut the benefit entitlement of existing claimants.

Business.title: Anthropic set for $1.3tn stock market debut despite 'catastrophic' AI warning
Business.text:
Anthropic, the artificial intelligence (AI) company behind the Claude chatbot, could be valued at around $1.3 trillion (£1 trillion) when it lists its shares for sale on New York's Nasdaq stock exchange.

The loss-making company says it will offer its shares for between $70 and $78 each and will raise up to $64bn when it floats this month.

It would value Anthropic at between $1.1tn and $1.3tn which, although large, is below the $2tn some backers of the firm predicted in summer, according to the Financial Times.

The huge valuation comes despite the company warning last month that AI could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity".

It is floating at a volatile time for big tech firms. After last week's US midterm elections, the Nasdaq fell sharply on concerns a Democrat-led Congress could slow development of AI and the buildout of data centres.

There are also wider fears over the billions of dollars being spent on AI and whether it will pay off.

In its most recent results for the six months to the end of June, Anthropic's revenues jumped to $16.2bn from $1.1bn in the same period last year.

However, its pre-tax loss jumped to $80.7bn from $12.9bn.

Fiona Cincotta, a senior market analyst at City Index, said the $64bn Anthropic wants to raise is "fairly bullish" within "the volatility [and] concerns towards AI that we've seen in sort of particularly last week".

She told Reuters: "It's showing that they are still sort of upbeat about the outlook as far as AI is concerned and that obviously that they think that the demand is going to be there."

Anthropic, which will list under the symbol ANT on 19 November, will be the first fully AI-focused company to go public, making it a test case for the future of the technology.

At $1.3tn, Anthropic's possible valuation is below SpaceX, Elon Musk's rocket, satellite and artificial intelligence company, which listed its shares in June and was valued at nearly $1.8tn.

Business.title: Tinned food and bottled water sales jump after 'Be Ready' campaign launch
Business.text:
Sales of essential goods such as bottled water and canned food soared in the 10 days following the launch of the government's "Be Ready" emergency preparedness campaign on 22 October, research indicates.

Hand sanitiser sales were up 83%, sales of bottled water rose 67% and tinned and jarred goods climbed 37%, according to data from retail research firm Worldpanel by Numerator.

The government's public awareness campaign encouraged people to stock up in case of disruption to essential services by severe weather or cyberattacks.

However, Worldpanel said that while households were stockpiling essentials, they were not panic buying.

The government campaign encouraged people to keep three days-worth of food and water in their homes.

Wet wipes, a torch and cash were also recommended.

After the campaign launch, the equivalent of an extra 400,000 people per day bought tinned meat, Worldpanel said, although the typical amount remained at 500g, which suggests a gradual stocking-up.

"Shoppers clearly took notice of the 'Be Ready' campaign, but this wasn't panic buying, with less than a third of households buying bottled water in October," said Fraser McKevitt, head of retail and consumer insight at Worldpanel by Numerator.

"Growth came from more people adding the recommended items on the government's checklist to their weekly shop, not from shoppers piling their trolleys high, which is very much in line with what the government wanted households to do," he said.

Sales of tinned and jarred goods rose from £58.2m in the 10 days to 2 November 2025 to £79.5m over the same period in 2026.

Bottled water sales jumped from £13.6m to £22.8m compared with a year earlier and hand sanitiser sales climbed from £497,000 to £908,000.

Business.title: Kim Kardashian's Skims offers refunds for $148 advent calendar after backlash
Business.text:
Kim Kardashian's Skims is offering customers refunds for its $148 (£110) advent calendar which has been widely criticised on social media.

The accessories advent calendar promised "twelve days of fun surprises" but has been mocked online for the quality of its contents, such as hair clips and keychains, with some comparing them to something you would find down the back of a sofa.

A spokesperson for Skims has told a number of media outlets "for some, the calendar didn't meet expectations" and the company has "personally contacted every customer" to offer a full refund or credit to put towards other products".

The BBC has contacted Skims for comment.

The shapewear and clothing business was co-founded by Kardashian in 2019 and has made the reality TV star a billionaire, according to Forbes magazine.

Skims was valued at $5bn in 2025 when it raised millions of dollars in new funding.

One account on TikTok called spicychathouse compared the contents of the calendar to things "my cat collects from around my house". Another account said it looked like "a bunch of stuff that Kim Kardashian was emptying out of her bedside table".

A number of accounts showed people cleaning out their own sofas and claiming they had accidentally created the Skims advent calendar.

"It is really interesting to see this kind of backlash," said Kate Vlietstra, senior director of food and drink at market research analyst Mintel.

"It is something we have been seeing a bit more in recent years, particularly with the trend for unboxing on social media," she said,

"It means that, inevitably, if people are not feeling they're getting the value that they have hoped for from the advent calendar...they've purchased, then yes, there is going to be a backlash."

Advent calendars remain popular, according to Helen Wing, head of innovation at market research company Ipsos though she said that "the buzz around them has reduced a little bit".

She said according to Ipsos research, people are willing to pay a bit more for an advent calendar but the contents have to justify the price tag.

Using a £285 advent calendar sold by Liberty as an example, Wing said the upmarket department story is "very open about the value of the contents".

"They will say there is over £1,000 worth of content," she said. "If you've got that reassurance when you're making the purchase, particularly if it is for a gift, then it is important to have some faith that the contents are actually going to be worth the money that you're paying."

Business.title: North Korean hackers used fake video calls in $400m crypto hack, says FBI
Business.text:
State-sponsored hackers from North Korea have taken more than $400 million in cryptocurrency by using fake video calls to steal people's identities, US authorities say.

More than 900 victims have fallen prey to the scheme, which the FBI refers to as FaceStealer, in the last 18 months, according to the bureau.

"The North Korean regime relies on proceeds from large-scale cryptocurrency theft to fund its illicit weapons program, stealing billions of dollars in recent years," says FBI cyber director Brett Leatherman.

This comes a week after the world's largest crypto exchange Binance revealed that hackers had used fake job interviews to steal a record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) from the company.

US law enforcement agencies attributed the Binance hack, thought to be the largest crypto hack to date, to North Korea-linked actors. Pyongyang has denied this claim.

Authorities say FaceStealer, the latest scheme, "aggressively targets" those who work in the cryptocurrency and web3 sectors, particularly those who are involved in the development and maintenance of open-source software.

According to the FBI and US Justice Department, FaceStealer hackers use fake or hijacked social media accounts to invite potential victims into video calls hosted over "imposter versions" of Zoom, Microsoft Teams, and Google Meet.

Next, the hackers play pre-recorded videos of previous victims the target is acquainted with to simulate a legitimate call – except that the audio would appear to malfunction.

A message then pops up on the target's screen, asking them to "fix" the audio by clicking on a link. This "fix" would eventually download malware onto the target's device, which allows hackers to access their contact lists and apps, widening their pool of potential victims.

Hackers would secretly record these calls and use the recordings as material to scam their new victims, according to the US authorities.

The FBI has described FaceStealer as "a highly effective social engineering scheme capable of deceiving even the most experienced technical and security conscious computer user".

"It exploits our trust in ubiquitous video conference platforms and valued personal relationships," Patrick Grandy, assistant director in charge of the bureau's Los Angeles field office, said in a statement on Thursday.

"If you can't imagine a scenario where you might fall prey to it, you are not thinking creatively enough."
